transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess... I mean, my daughter is the one who drove me here. She has this blue sedan, very reliable, not like the old clunker I used to drive back in the 90s. That thing broke down on the highway twice. But anyway, she insisted I come. What scared me enough to actually agree to it is... well, I just keep thinking it would be such a relief if I just went to sleep and didn't wake up. I haven't tried to hurt myself or anything like that, but the thought is just... there. It's like how my neighbor's dog just lays on the porch all day, not moving, just waiting. I don't know, it's just heavy.
Have you noticed that you don't enjoy things as much as you used to, or have lost interest in activities you once found pleasurable?

I suppose I have, yes. I used to really look forward to my watercolors... I had this nice set, the kind that come in those little metal tubes. My sister bought them for me a few years back. She always gives the best gifts, you know, she got me this real silk scarf last year that I wore to my niece's wedding. It was an outdoor wedding, and it practically rained on us, but thank goodness they had a tent set up near the buffet... anyway, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, the paints. I just leave my things sitting there on the dining table now. I just can't make myself care to open them. It's the same with my dance class, and walking with the ladies. Brenda from the walking group just had knee surgery, actually. They put a whole metal joint in her leg. I can't imagine going through that, the physical therapy sounds just awful... but well, I haven't even been walking with them anyway. I just don't care to go.
How long have you been feeling this way, with a loss of interest in things you used to enjoy and thoughts of not waking up?

I'd say it's been... oh, about four months now. It started right around the time my aunt came to live with us. She had to leave her place down in Florida, you know, the homeowners association raised the fees so high she just couldn't afford it on her fixed income. It's an absolute shame what they do to folks down there. So she packed up and brought all this heavy oak furniture with her. It took up half our garage! My son-in-law had to help unload it all, and he actually pulled a muscle in his lower back doing it. He was out of work for a whole week, and he works over at the hardware store, so he's on his feet all day and really needs his back to be right... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, how long. Yes, about four months. Ever since she moved in, really.
Have these feelings been present most days, and have they been continuous over these four months, or have they come and gone?

I... I'm not really sure, to be honest. I don't really keep track. The days just sort of blur together now. Like yesterday was Tuesday, and I only know that because the garbage truck comes on Tuesdays. Though they changed their route a few weeks ago. It used to be they'd come right at 7 AM, making all that racket and waking everybody up. Now they don't show up until nearly noon. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he gets so fired up about it because he likes to bring his bins in before he goes to his afternoon shift. He works over at the bottling factory, you know, the one off Route 9? They make that ginger ale with the green label... my husband used to drink that whenever his stomach was upset. He absolutely swore by it, said it was the only thing that settled him. 

But anyway... what was the question? If it comes and goes? I really couldn't tell you. I just haven't paid enough attention to know if there are breaks in it or not. I'm just not sure.
Would you say that your mood has been persistently down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, over these past four months?

Well, yes... I suppose so. Most mornings I wake up with this heavy sadness right here in my chest, like I've already failed the day before it even starts. It's just sitting there. I usually wake up pretty early, around 5:30. That's when the paperboy comes by. He's a new boy, maybe fourteen or fifteen, and he rides this bright orange bicycle. It has those little reflectors on the spokes that catch the streetlight. My brother had a bike just like that when we were kids. We used to ride all the way down to the creek at the end of our road and catch tadpoles in these old mayonnaise jars. Mother would get so cross with us because we'd track mud all over the linoleum floor. She spent half her life scrubbing that floor, I swear. She had this special pine cleaner she bought from a man who sold it out of the trunk of his car... 

Oh, what was I saying? Right, the sadness. Yes, it's there most of the day, pretty much every day. Just heavy.
Have you noticed that you've been moving more slowly than usual, or that it takes you longer to get things done? Or on the flip side, have you felt restless or fidgety, unable to sit still?

Well, my husband has been saying something about that. He tells me I move like everything takes extra effort now, like I'm wading through molasses or something. Even when we go to the market... I'll just stand there in the aisle, looking at the shelves, and it takes me entirely too long to just pick up the can of soup I came for. The market has been so crowded lately, too. They started doing this new promotion on Thursdays, double coupons or something like that, and the parking lot is just a nightmare. Last week, I saw a woman back her station wagon right into one of those cart corrals. Left a terrible dent in her bumper. It was a blue wagon, sort of a powder blue, like the color we painted the nursery when my daughter was born. We couldn't decide between yellow and blue, but the man at the hardware store mixed up the blue by mistake, so he gave it to us for half price. My husband was thrilled because money was so tight back then, what with him just starting out at the plant...

I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, moving slow. Yes, I suppose I do. Just standing there at the market, unable to move on.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating much less or more than usual, or losing or gaining weight without trying?

I haven't really noticed any changes, no. I mean, I eat when my husband puts something in front of me, I suppose. He made meatloaf last night. He uses that recipe from the back of the oatmeal box, the one with the little Quaker man on it. I always thought that man looked a bit like my Uncle Arthur, especially around the eyes. Uncle Arthur used to wear those little wire-rimmed glasses, and he'd sit on the porch smoking his pipe. It was cherry tobacco, I think. You could smell it all the way down the street when the wind was right. He had this old hound dog named Buster who would just lay there at his feet all day, thumping his tail whenever a car went by. Buster was terrified of thunderstorms, though. One time, it stormed so bad the power went out for two days, and we had to eat all the ice cream out of the freezer so it wouldn't go bad... 

I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. Weight? No, my clothes seem to fit the same as they always do. I haven't noticed anything different.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty about things you've done, or feeling like you're not worth much, or maybe even feeling like you're a burden to others?

Well, yes. I do get to feeling terribly guilty. Like with my aunt... sometimes I just get so tired, or I get annoyed with her, and I start thinking I'm just a bad woman. She always wants her tea at exactly three o'clock, you see. And it has to be in this specific china cup with little pink roses painted on the side. My grandmother gave her that cup. Grandma had a whole set of them, actually, a beautiful set, but most of them got broken during the big move back in '78. We moved right in the middle of a terrible snowstorm. The moving truck got stuck at the bottom of our hill, and those poor men had to carry everything up by hand in the freezing cold. One of them slipped on a patch of black ice and dropped a whole box of kitchen things... it sounded like a chandelier crashing to the floor. He felt just awful about it, but my husband gave him some hot coffee from a thermos and told him not to fret. It was one of those old metal thermoses, plaid, red and black... my husband used to take it to the plant every single day before they put in the new cafeteria... 

Oh, excuse me. I'm rambling again. You asked about feeling guilty. Yes... when I get annoyed with my aunt like that, I just feel like I'm bringing shame on my whole family for not being more grateful. I really am a bad woman for feeling that way.
Have you noticed that you feel more tired than usual, or like you don't have any energy, even after resting?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. Even after a full night in bed, my body just feels so worn out. Like just carrying the laundry basket or trying to make breakfast takes so much more out of me than it should. The laundry basket I have is one of those tall wicker ones, you know? It's lined with this lovely white cotton cloth that ties at the corners. I bought it at a little craft fair over at the Methodist church... oh, it must have been ten years ago now. They always have such nice things there. Mrs. Higgins, the lady who runs the bake sale table, she makes these incredible pecan sandies. They just melt in your mouth. She uses real butter, none of that margarine nonsense. My mother used to say margarine was just one step away from plastic, and she refused to let it in the house. She was very particular about her baking, my mother. She had this heavy cast-iron skillet she used for everything, even cornbread. The cornbread always came out with this perfect, crispy crust on the bottom... 

I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, being tired. Yes, just making breakfast feels like such a chore these days. I just don't have the energy I used to.
Have you noticed that your thoughts have been slower than usual, or that it's harder for you to focus or make decisions, even about small things?

I don't think so, no. I mean, I can still make up my mind just fine. Like yesterday, I was at the market trying to decide which soap to buy. They have so many kinds now, all those bright colored bottles and strange scents. I usually just stick to the Ivory bars. You know, Ivory soap floats in the water. My brother Tommy and I used to play with it in the old clawfoot tub we had growing up. That tub was so deep, it felt like a whole swimming pool when we were little. Tommy had this plastic yellow tugboat he'd push around the soap. He got it for his birthday from our Uncle Henry. Uncle Henry worked on the railroad, you see. He always wore those thick striped overalls and he kept a big silver pocket watch tucked right in the front bib pocket. He'd pull it out and click it open for us, and it had the most beautiful, steady ticking sound. He used to tell us that if you listened close enough to the ticking, you could hear the freight train coming down the tracks... 

Oh, listen to me going on. I'm sorry, my mind just wanders off into memories sometimes. But no, to answer your question, my thoughts don't feel slow or anything. I haven't noticed any real trouble focusing or deciding on things.
Would you say that your lack of energy or feeling of constant fatigue has been present most of the day, nearly every day, for these past four months?

Well, yes, I'd say so. It's been going on for about four months, ever since my aunt came to live with us. We had to put her in the front bedroom because she can't manage the stairs anymore. That room gets such beautiful morning light, you know. I used to have my ironing board set up in there, right by the window. I had this heavy old iron, a Sunbeam, with a thick black handle. They just don't make them like that anymore. The new ones are all light plastic and they just don't press a collar the same way. My husband, bless his heart, he always needed his collars pressed perfectly for church on Sundays. He would wear this handsome navy blue suit... he bought it at a little men's shop downtown that closed years and years ago. Mr. Henderson ran that shop, and he always kept a little crystal bowl of peppermint candies on the glass counter. Those soft ones that just melt on your tongue, with the red stripes... 

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry, my mind just takes off on me. But yes, to answer you, it's been about four months of feeling that tired every single day, right since she moved in.
Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating, like trouble following conversations or remembering things that used to be easy for you?

No, I haven't really noticed any trouble like that. I can still follow along with what people are saying just fine. Like when my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, comes over for tea. We talk for hours sometimes. She always brings these little lemon cookies she gets from the bakery down on Main Street. The bakery has this big red awning over the door, and a little bell that jingles when you walk in. I love that sound. It reminds me of the bell on the collar of my first cat, Mittens. She was a tuxedo cat, black with little white paws, like she was wearing socks. She used to sleep right at the foot of my bed on this old patchwork quilt my grandmother made. It was made from scraps of all my childhood dresses, lots of pinks and yellows. There was one square from my favorite Easter dress, the one with the little embroidered daisies on the collar...

Oh, dear, I've wandered off again, haven't I? I apologize. But no, I haven't had any trouble concentrating or remembering things. My memory is still sharp as a tack.
Have you found it harder lately to focus on tasks, follow conversations, or make decisions, even about small things?

I feel like we might have just talked about this, didn't we? But no, making decisions and focusing isn't hard at all. Just this morning I had to decide what to wear to come see you, and it was easy as pie. I picked out this floral blouse because it has these little pearl buttons down the front. I've always loved pearl buttons. My grandmother had a whole tin of buttons she kept in her sewing room. It was an old Royal Dansk butter cookie tin, you know the blue ones? We always hoped there would be cookies inside, but it was always just threads and needles and hundreds of loose buttons. She had this one big shiny black button that looked exactly like a beetle. I used to pretend it was a real bug crawling around the fabric scraps while she worked. She was making a wedding dress for my cousin Mary... 

Oh, goodness me, I'm doing it again. I just get so caught up in these pictures in my head, they just take over. I'm sorry. But no, I promise my focus is fine and I don't have any trouble deciding on things.
Would you say that you’ve completely lost interest in most things, to the point where nothing really brings you any pleasure anymore?

Well, yes, I suppose that's true. I just... I don't care about much of anything right now. I used to look forward to my watercolors so much. I had this little set of Windsor and Newton paints, the ones in the little half-pans, you know? They came in a black metal tin that folded out so you could mix the colors on the lid. I always loved mixing sap green with just a tiny touch of burnt umber to get the perfect color for pine trees. We used to go up to the mountains every autumn, my husband and I, to a little cabin near a lake. The water was so clear you could see the smooth stones on the bottom, all gray and white. We'd collect the prettiest ones and bring them home to put in the garden around the rose bushes. My mother planted those roses when we first bought the house. They were Peace roses, the big yellow ones with the pink edges on the petals. They smelled like... like heaven, really. 

Oh, listen to me, I'm miles away again. I'm sorry. But yes, the watercolors just sit there now. And my dance class, and walking with the ladies in the neighborhood... I just leave my things sitting there and I can't make myself care about any of it anymore.
Would you say that you’ve completely lost interest in all or almost all activities, to the point where nothing really brings you any pleasure anymore?

We just talked about this, didn't we? I... I'm pretty sure we did. But yes, it's like I said, I just don't have the heart for anything anymore. Not the watercolors, not the dancing... I used to love dancing. My husband, Frank, he had two left feet, bless him, but he'd always take me to the Moose Lodge on Saturday nights because they had a live band. They always played "Moon River" at the end of the night. Frank would step on my toes, but he'd smile that crooked smile of his. He chipped his front tooth when he was ten, falling off a bicycle he built out of spare parts from the junkyard. He was always tinkering with things, hands covered in grease. He smelled like motor oil and Old Spice... 

Oh, dear me. I've done it again, haven't I? My mind just drifts off to these old memories. I'm sorry, Doctor. But yes, to answer your question, nothing really brings me any joy these days. I just don't care about the things I used to do.
Would you say that you’ve completely lost interest in absolutely everything, to the point where nothing at all brings you any pleasure anymore, not even things you used to really enjoy?

Doctor, I really feel like I'm losing my mind a bit, didn't you just ask me this? Or maybe it was just a minute ago? I'm sorry, my head is just... well, anyway. Yes. Everything. It's exactly like I was saying about my watercolors, they're just gathering dust. And my walking shoes are sitting right by the front door, right on that little woven rug I bought at the craft fair. The lady who made it was so sweet, she used all recycled fabrics, mostly old denim jeans. You could see the little brass rivets peeking out if you looked closely. I always thought it was so clever to turn something worn out into something beautiful like that. I used to make quilts out of my kids' old clothes when they were little. I made this one for my daughter with all her old corduroy overalls, it was so heavy and warm. She used to drag it around everywhere until the binding started falling off...

Oh, for heaven's sake, there I go again. I'm so sorry. I just get lost in my own head. But to answer you, yes, I've completely lost interest. The watercolors, the dancing, the walking... I just can't make myself care about any of it anymore.
Have you ever felt this way before—like you've lost interest in everything and nothing brings you joy—or is this the first time you've experienced these kinds of feelings?

No, I don't think so. I mean, everyone gets the blues sometimes, but never like this. I've always been someone who could find a little bit of joy in things, even when times were tough. Like when I had to leave high school early to help out my Aunt Betty. She ran a little bakery downtown, and she broke her hip slipping on some ice. It was a terrible winter that year, the snow was piled up past the windowsills. We had to shovel a path just to get to the front door of the shop. 

We made these cherry turnovers that were just famous in our neighborhood. The secret was putting a tiny drop of almond extract in the sugar glaze. Aunt Betty used to let me do the glazing, and I'd use this big pastry brush with wooden bristles. It looked like a paintbrush, really. Sometimes I'd pretend I was painting a masterpiece instead of just frosting pastries. The smell of that almond and the warm cherries... it would fill up the whole block. Mr. Henderson from the hardware store next door would come in every morning at 10 sharp, checking his silver pocket watch. It had a little bald eagle engraved on the front...

Oh, Lord, I'm doing it again. I'm so sorry, Doctor. My brain just wanders off down memory lane and I can't seem to stop it. But no, to answer your question, this is the first time it's ever been like this. Even when things were hard back then, I still enjoyed the baking and seeing the customers. Now, I just don't have it in me to care.

inference_history.note: The patient's symptoms, including persistent thoughts of death, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, and psychosocial clues, point toward a major depressive episode. There is no clear evidence yet to distinguish between a single episode and recurrent episodes, so both F32 and F33 categories remain under consideration.

The patient reported a persistent low mood and loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities lasting approximately four months, without evidence of mania or psychosis. This duration and symptom profile makes major depressive disorder (recurrent or single episode, mild to moderate) more likely, narrowing the field. Rule out very mild (F32.0/F33.0) due to functional impairment and presence of suicidal ideation, but not severe (F32.2/F32.3/F33.2/F33.3) due to lack of psychomotor disturbance, psychosis, or severe functional impairment.

The patient continues to endorse persistent depressive symptoms including loss of interest in all activities, feelings of worthlessness, fatigue, and psychomotor slowing. The absence of a significant change in appetite or weight, and the lack of concentration difficulties, help rule out some specifiers but support the presence of moderate to severe depressive episodes. The chronicity and severity support the continued consideration of F32.2 (Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe without psychotic features) and F33.2 (Recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe without psychotic features). The patient has not endorsed psychotic features, and there's insufficient evidence to suggest a bipolar etiology.
